R3:physical.title: Kilometre-scale weather and climate
R3:physical.summary: COMPUTE-BOUND. km-scale grids let convection be simulated rather than parameterized. ICON at 1 km is about 1500x short of 1 simulated year per day, and even a pre-exascale-sized machine reaches only about 0.06 SYPD. I/O and storage are an emerging limit. ML (GenCast: a 15-day ensemble in 8 min) changes the cost curve, because the atmosphere's state is observed.

R3:physical.title: Ensemble data assimilation of fault stress (boundary case)
R3:physical.summary: NOT COMPUTE-BOUND on the real Earth. A synthetic 2-D perfect-model test with 150 members forecast 70% of 21 events with the alarm on 17% of the time, against 68% for a periodic model. The runs were nearly embarrassingly parallel and about 20 members sufficed. On real faults, model error and unobserved deep stress (C2) bind first.

roots.question: Can scientific paper reviews (maybe specifically ML, DL, data-driven papers) be automated with highly scoped, small subagents following the AISLE model: many open-source models, since they have different blind spots, with tasks scoped to known failure modes like biases, factual reproduction errors, 'do these authors/papers exist' errors and overclaims, including building the suggested experiments and variations and running them on GPUs? Is compute a major blocker at some level, could a shit ton of GPU parallelism fix it?

What's actually stopping general purpose robot hands from reliably doing stuff like folding laundry or loading a dishwasher? Is it the lack of real-world manipulation data, the hardware (sensors, actuators, tactile feedback), or the sim-to-real gap? Is that a major blocker at some level, and could it be fixed by running millions of simulated robots in parallel on a shit ton of GPUs?

Why can't we predict earthquakes days or hours in advance? Is it fundamentally chaotic physics that no model can get around, or is it mostly a data problem with too few sensors and too few big quakes to learn from? Could training huge foundation models on decades of global seismic waveforms, GPS strain and fault simulations with a shit ton of GPU parallelism actually get somewhere, or is compute not the blocker at all?

What actually stops us from autoformalizing most of published math into Lean? Is it gaps in Mathlib coverage, the step of translating informal proofs where authors skip things that are 'obvious', or something deeper about how mathematicians write? The Lean kernel is a free and perfect verifier, so this looks like one of the few domains where brute-force search can't fool itself. Could you split every paper into tiny lemma-sized subgoals and throw many different open-source prover models at each one in parallel, with each model scoped to a known failure mode like wrong definitions, mismatched conventions or silently strengthened hypotheses? Is compute a major blocker at some level, and could a shit ton of GPU parallelism fix it, or is the real bottleneck checking that the formal statement means the same thing as the English one?

What limits general-purpose robot manipulation right now? Is it lack of real-world data, the sim-to-real gap, or hardware like hands and tactile sensors? If you can already run millions of simulated environments in parallel on GPUs with heavy domain randomization, why can't you brute-force a policy that folds laundry or ties knots and then transfers to a real robot? Is contact and deformable-object physics the wall that no amount of compute gets you over because the simulator itself is wrong in ways you can't randomize away? Or could a shit ton of GPU parallelism plus a small fleet of real robots that keeps correcting the simulator close the loop?

pick.title: Ensemble data assimilation of fault stress (boundary case)

plan.option_title: Ensemble data assimilation of fault stress (boundary case)
plan.question: On a synthetic benchmark fault, does earthquake-forecast skill keep rising as the assimilation ensemble grows, or does it level off early while model error and sensor depth decide?
plan.hypothesis: Skill levels off at tens to hundreds of members, because model error and depth of data limit it first, as the one perfect-model study [van_dinther] suggests.

compute_axis.quantity: ensemble size M (members per ensemble Kalman filter or particle filter run)

held_fixed: SEAS BP1/BP2-style fault: 1,600 cells at 25 m, FP64, aging law
Main truth D_c = 2 mm plus Ornstein-Uhlenbeck normal-stress noise (2% std, 10 yr correlation)
5 independent truths, each 1,500 yr with 500 yr spin-up, 1,000 yr assimilated
Observation noise 1 mm/yr on annual means; 1-year assimilation window by default
Alarm rule and Molchan area skill score metric

predictions.if_lever: Skill is still rising beyond 1,024 members in the model-error or particle-filter arms, by more than the gain from deep stress data.
predictions.if_not: Skill plateaus at 256 members or fewer in every ensemble Kalman filter arm; model error or deep data changes skill more than going from 32 members to the largest.
predictions.decision_rule: M* = smallest M whose area skill score is within one standard error of the score at the largest M. W11 holds if M* <= 256 in every EnKF arm (E1, E2) and the skill lost to model error or gained from deep data exceeds the gain from M=32 to the largest M. Contradicted if in E2 or E4 the score still rises beyond M=1,024 by more than the E3 deep-data gain.
predictions.noise_rule: Area skill score averaged over 5 independent truths, with standard error across truths; M* defined within one standard error.
predictions.expected_why: The file expects skill to level off at tens to hundreds of members, with only the particle-filter arm plausibly continuing to gain.

plan.compute_tested_why: Ensemble size M, which parallel GPUs buy, is varied from 16 to 16,384 members, about 100 times beyond the published studies.
plan.scored_against: Molchan diagram area skill score of forecasts of full-rupture events in the hidden synthetic truth, compared with Poisson, periodic-recurrence, pattern-repeat, open-loop and oracle baselines.

checks: V1 kernel: uniform slip plus creeping extension gives zero stress, relative residual < 1e-6 (pilot gave 4e-16)

records.card: **W11 · Ensemble data assimilation of fault stress (boundary case).** R3 · physical · random pick · compute tested: yes · plan expects: not the lever **Question.** On a synthetic benchmark fault, does earthquake-forecast skill keep rising as the assimilation ensemble grows, or does it level off early while model error and sensor depth decide? **What is known.** van Dinther et al. 2019 ran an ensemble Kalman filter with 150 members on a 2-D subduction analogue; Diab-Montero et al. 2023 used 50 members on a single-point 1-D fault model with perfect model. Forecast skill versus ensemble size beyond 150 members, under model error, on a depth-resolved rate-and-state fault, with EnKF compared against a large particle filter. **Hypothesis.** Skill levels off at tens to hundreds of members, because model error and depth of data limit it first, as the one perfect-model study [van_dinther] suggests. **Restructuring.** Each member's adaptive time stepping through earthquakes: thousands of steps per event, up to about 8,050 accepted steps per cycle. Thousands of independent members run as columns of one batched matrix on GPU; finished members are gathered into smaller batches every 32 steps so slow ruptures do not stall the rest. **If compute is the lever.** Skill is still rising beyond 1,024 members in the model-error or particle-filter arms, by more than the gain from deep stress data. **If not.** Skill plateaus at 256 members or fewer in every ensemble Kalman filter arm; model error or deep data changes skill more than going from 32 members to the largest. **Test.** Run thousands of copies of a benchmark earthquake fault on GPUs inside ensemble Kalman and particle filters. Measure forecast skill against ensemble size, with and without model error and deep sensors, against simple baselines [van_dinther]. *Compute axis.* Ensemble size M (members per ensemble Kalman filter or particle filter run): 16–16,384 members, 10 levels. Closest prior: 150 [van_dinther], beyond it. Prior art checked without web search. **Check first.** A single-member run of the first benchmark fault at 25 m reproduces an independent code, QDYN: recurrence interval and first-event time within 1%, slip-rate series overlay at benchmark stations. Tolerance: within 1% on recurrence interval and first-event time. **Would not show.** A plateau would confirm the hypothesis only for synthetic data from a known model class, not the real Earth. GPU timings are assumptions until Phase 0b; truth noise amplitude is tuned, not observed. *Cost.* Plans $684.14 of the $1,000 budget over 26 machine-hours, leaving $315.86.
